introduction: Humility raises a person and pride brings them down; real strength shows itself as meekness; whoever serves is greatest; and before God a human being is poor, weak and nothing. The guide says these things in counsel, in stories of people who lived them, and in many prayers. A hundred of its quotations are read here with a hundred from elsewhere. The Hebrew prophets and psalms, the Gospels and Paul say the same in nearly the same words: walk humbly, take the lowest room, the meek shall inherit, what hast thou that thou didst not receive. Lao Tzu’s rivers rule the valleys by lying below them; Confucius distinguishes dignified ease from pride; Socrates is wiser only in knowing that he does not know; the Qur’an tells its Prophet to lower his wing. The critics of humility are heard too. Aristotle thinks undue humility a fault, Whitman and Emerson praise the self, Nietzsche wants greatness, Wollstonecraft warns against teaching submission to girls, and Franklin observes that one can be proud of one’s humility. Jesus himself is the sharpest critic of a humility that is performed.
questions: The guide says that humility exalts and pride abases. What experience of your own bears this out, or seems to contradict it?
Aristotle thinks a person can claim too little for themselves. How is humility different from having a low opinion of one's abilities?
Many of the prayers here speak of being nothing before God. What is the difference between that confession and thinking oneself worthless?
Franklin says he would probably be proud of his humility. How does one grow in a virtue that is spoiled by noticing it?
The guide asks those in authority to be known by humility and service. Whom have you known who held authority in that way?
Jesus warns against taking the lowest seat for show. How can a community honour humility without rewarding the appearance of it?

outside.why: Micah says that what is required is to do justly, to love mercy and to walk humbly with thy God.
Jesus says of giving that the left hand should not know what the right hand does.
Jesus says: learn of me, for I am meek and lowly in heart, and ye shall find rest unto your souls.
James quotes the saying that God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.
Isaiah's high and lofty One dwells with him that is of a contrite and humble spirit.
Jesus says: blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.
Jesus tells a host to invite the poor, the maimed and the blind, who cannot recompense him.
Shakespeare's Isabella says it is excellent to have a giant's strength, but tyrannous to use it like a giant. What does it take for the strong to choose meekness?
Proverbs says that pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
Aristotle counts undue humility a fault: the unduly humble man falls short in comparison with his own merits. Can a person think too little of themselves, and how would humility differ from that?
The Qur'an uses the same phrase: lower thy wing unto the believers.
Proverbs says that the fear of the Lord is the instruction of wisdom, and before honour is humility.
Lao Tzu says that rivers and seas receive the tribute of all the valley streams through their skill in being lower than they.
Abraham, taking it upon himself to speak to the Lord, calls himself but dust and ashes.
Jesus, having washed his disciples' feet, says: I have given you an example, that ye should do as I have done to you.
Jesus advises a guest to sit down in the lowest room, so that he may be told to go up higher. Is a humility chosen in the hope of being exalted still humility?
Paul asks believers to be kindly affectioned one to another, in honour preferring one another.
The Qur'an describes the servants of the Beneficent as those who walk upon the earth modestly and answer the foolish with 'Peace'.
Socrates finds himself better off than a man reputed wise only in this: I neither know nor think that I know.
Whitman declares: divine am I inside and out, and I make holy whatever I touch. Is the confession of one's poverty the essence of understanding, or is there understanding in his boast too?
Paul says of Christ that he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death.
Wollstonecraft wanted the female mind strengthened so that blind obedience might end. How is a humility taught to girls to be kept from becoming the submission she opposed?
Jesus says that unless ye become as little children ye shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.
Mark says that whoever does not receive the kingdom as a little child shall not enter therein.
Jesus says: he that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone.
Jesus asks why one beholds the mote in a brother's eye and considers not the beam in one's own.
Proverbs says: let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth.
James rebukes a congregation that gives the good place to the man in fine clothing and tells the poor man to stand.
Paul says that Christ came to save sinners, of whom I am chief.
Isaiah's servant is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and opens not his mouth.
Deuteronomy has even the king keep a copy of the law beside him all the days of his life.
The Preacher says: God is in heaven, and thou upon earth, therefore let thy words be few.
Paul's image for an unbroken circle is the body, whose many members are one.
Jesus says that whoever will be great among you shall be your minister.
Zechariah's king comes to his city just and lowly, and riding upon an ass.
Macbeth has no spur but vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself and falls on the other side.
Numbers says that the man Moses was very meek, above all the men upon the face of the earth.
John the Baptist says of the one coming after him that he is not worthy to unloose his shoe's latchet.
Peter falls at Jesus's knees and says: depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord.
Franklin admits that if he ever overcame his pride he would probably be proud of his humility. How does a person practise humility without watching themselves do it?
Jesus tells his disciples, when they have done all, to say: we are unprofitable servants.
Jesus says: I am the vine, ye are the branches, and without me ye can do nothing.
Paul asks: what hast thou that thou didst not receive, and why glory as if thou hadst not received it?
Paul says: by the grace of God I am what I am, and I laboured, yet not I, but the grace of God.
Paul tells every man not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think soberly.
Emerson says: trust thyself, every heart vibrates to that iron string. Is self-trust the vanity an intelligent person avoids, or something else?
The psalm says that God knows our frame and remembers that we are dust.
Jesus counts what is done for the hungry, the stranger and the sick as done to himself.
Job, having seen, says: I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes. Is self-abhorrence what the guide means by regarding oneself as nothing, and can it be healthy?
Paul asks that in lowliness of mind each esteem other better than themselves.
Mary sings that God has regarded the low estate of his handmaiden.
The psalmist would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of his God than dwell in the tents of wickedness.
Isaiah counts the nations as a drop of a bucket and the small dust of the balance.
Paul was told that strength is made perfect in weakness, and gloried in his infirmities.
In the parable the man who will not lift his eyes and says 'God be merciful to me a sinner' goes home justified.
Paul tells those called to liberty not to use it for themselves, but by love to serve one another.
The psalmist considers the heavens and asks: what is man, that thou art mindful of him?
Peter's letter says: be clothed with humility, and humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God.
Moses pleads that he is slow of speech and of a slow tongue.
The Qur'an says: O mankind, ye are the poor in your relation to God.
Jesus says: blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
Confucius says that the superior man has a dignified ease without pride, and the mean man has pride without a dignified ease.
Job answers: behold, I am vile; I will lay mine hand upon my mouth.
Isaiah prays: we are the clay, and thou our potter, and we all are the work of thy hand.
The psalm says that a broken and a contrite heart God will not despise.
Habakkuk says: the Lord is in his holy temple, let all the earth keep silence before him.
The psalm says that he has not dealt with us after our sins.
The Dhammapada says that the fool who knows his foolishness is wise at least so far.
Pope says: know then thyself, presume not God to scan; the proper study of mankind is man.
Spinoza holds that all things are in God and cannot be conceived without him. Is the confession of powerlessness in these prayers a feeling to be cultivated, or a fact to be understood?
Isaiah hears: to this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit.
The Qur'an says: walk not in the earth exultant, for thou canst not rend the earth nor match the hills in height.
The psalmist says that his heart is not haughty, nor does he exercise himself in things too high for him.
Augustine says that our hearts are restless until they rest in God.
Paul reminds his church that not many wise, mighty or noble are called, and that God has chosen the weak things of the world.
John the Baptist says of the one he announced: he must increase, but I must decrease.
Jesus warns against doing good deeds before men, to be seen of them.
Milton says that God does not need man's work, and that they also serve who only stand and wait.
The Qur'an assigns the abode of the Hereafter to those who seek not exaltation in the earth.
Paul asks whether he seeks to please men, and says that if he did he would not be a servant.
Kipling wrote of his country's navies melting away and all its pomp of yesterday being one with Nineveh and Tyre.
Paul speaks of ordinances that have a show of wisdom in humility. How is a true humbling before God told from a show of it?
Jesus asks one who calls him good master: why callest thou me good? there is none good but one.
Paul says that to the weak he became as weak, that he might gain the weak.
Bunyan's shepherd boy sings that he that is down needs fear no fall, and he that is low, no pride.
Jesus says that the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister.
Chaucer's parson gave his flock this example, that first he wrought and afterward he taught.
Proverbs says that a word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver.
The psalm leaves praise to the heavens, which declare the glory of God.
Luke names the women who ministered to Jesus and the twelve of their substance.
Paul warns: let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.
In the parable the son has only begun to return when his father runs to meet him.
Paul says the treasure is in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God and not of us.
The psalmist prays before he speaks: O Lord, open thou my lips, and my mouth shall show forth thy praise.
Jesus sends his messengers on foot with neither purse nor scrip nor shoes.
Peter's letter recalls one who, when he was reviled, reviled not again.
Paul says: I have planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase.
Jesus speaks of those who love the uppermost rooms at feasts and the chief seats.
Jesus speaks of those who appear righteous outwardly and within are full of hypocrisy. What is the difference between taking the lowest seat and performing the taking of it?
Nietzsche calls man a rope stretched between the animal and the Superman. What would a teacher who prized greatness of soul above all say of the humility praised in this guide?

luke-take-the-lowest-room.text: When thou art bidden of any man to a wedding, sit not down in the highest room; lest a more honourable man than thou be bidden of him; And he that bade thee and him come and say to thee, Give this man place; and thou begin with shame to take the lowest room. But when thou art bidden, go and sit down in the lowest room; that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher: then shalt thou have worship in the presence of them that sit at meat with thee. For whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted

peter-clothed-with-humility.text: Likewise, ye younger, submit yourselves unto the elder. Yea, all of you be subject one to another, and be clothed with humility: for God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble. Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time

proverbs-pride-goeth-before-destruction.text: Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall. Better it is to be of an humble spirit with the lowly, than to divide the spoil with the proud

proverbs-before-honour-is-humility.text: The fear of the Lord is the instruction of wisdom; and before honour is humility

psalm-broken-and-contrite-heart.text: The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise

job-i-abhor-myself.text: I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee. Wherefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes

genesis-dust-and-ashes.text: And Abraham answered and said, Behold now, I have taken upon me to speak unto the Lord, which am but dust and ashes

luke-depart-from-me.text: When Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord

timothy-of-whom-i-am-chief.text: This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief

job-lay-mine-hand-upon-my-mouth.text: Behold, I am vile; what shall I answer thee? I will lay mine hand upon my mouth

matthew-uppermost-rooms-at-feasts.text: But all their works they do for to be seen of men: they make broad their phylacteries, and enlarge the borders of their garments, And love the uppermost rooms at feasts, and the chief seats in the synagogues, And greetings in the markets, and to be called of men, Rabbi, Rabbi

isaiah-to-this-man-will-i-look.text: For all those things hath mine hand made, and all those things have been, saith the Lord: but to this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word

james-god-resisteth-the-proud.text: But he giveth more grace. Wherefore he saith, God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble

quran-walk-not-in-the-land-exultant.text: And walk not in the earth exultant. Lo! thou canst not rend the earth, nor canst thou stretch to the height of the hills.

quran-lower-thy-wing-unto-the-believers.text: Strain not thine eyes toward that which We cause some wedded pairs among them to enjoin, and be not grieved on their account, and lower thy wing (in tenderness) for the believers.

quran-seek-not-oppression-in-the-earth.text: As for that Abode of the Hereafter We assign it unto those who seek not oppression in the earth, nor yet corruption. The sequel is for those who ward off (evil).

dhammapada-fool-who-knows-his-foolishnes.text: The fool who knows his foolishness, is wise at least so far. But a fool who thinks himself wise, he is called a fool indeed

shakespeare-giants-strength.text: it is excellent / To have a giant's strength; but it is tyrannous / To use it like a giant
shakespeare-giants-strength.author: William Shakespeare

tao-rivers-and-seas-kings-of-the-valleys.text: That whereby the rivers and seas are able to receive the homage and tribute of all the valley streams, is their skill in being lower than they
tao-rivers-and-seas-kings-of-the-valleys.author: Laozi

analects-dignified-ease-without-pride.text: The superior man has a dignified ease without pride. The mean man has pride without a dignified ease
analects-dignified-ease-without-pride.author: Confucius

plato-neither-know-nor-think-that-i-know.text: Well, although I do not suppose that either of us knows anything really beautiful and good, I am better off than he is - for he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows. I neither know nor think that I know
plato-neither-know-nor-think-that-i-know.author: Plato

aristotle-unduly-humble-man.text: The unduly humble man falls short both in comparison with his own merits and in comparison with the proud man's claims
aristotle-unduly-humble-man.author: Aristotle

franklin-proud-of-my-humility.text: For even if I could conceive that I had completely overcome it, I should probably be proud of my Humility
franklin-proud-of-my-humility.author: Benjamin Franklin
